title: Build a starter emergency fund ($1,000 or one month of expenses)
summary: A small buffer so the first unexpected expense doesn't become new debt.
detailsHtml:
Why this number

The starter EF is not your full reserve — it is the firebreak that keeps a flat tire, a vet bill, or a small medical co-pay from going on a credit card at 24% APR. The full emergency fund (Phase 5) comes later, after capturing the employer match and eliminating high-rate debt.

Where to keep it: A high-yield savings account (HYSA) or money market fund. As of May 2026, top-tier HYSA APYs run roughly 4–5% (NerdWallet's headline rate is 4.20% at Newtek; Bankrate's top tracked rate is 4.10%; Investopedia/Forbes show 5.00% available at Varo and AdelFi) — meaningfully above the FDIC national savings average of ~0.38–0.61%. The headline rate decays as the Fed cuts (the Fed funds target was 3.50–3.75% as of April 2026, down from the 2023–2024 peaks); verify current top-tier APYs against rate trackers (Bankrate, NerdWallet, DepositAccounts) at the time you actually act, since the rate environment shifts faster than this document is revised. Forward-rate expectation (two-sided): if Fed funds compress toward neutral-rate estimates (~2.5–3%) over the next 18–24 months, expect top-tier HYSA APYs to compress correspondingly toward ~2.5–3.5%; if inflation re-accelerates (as mid-2026 prints suggested was possible), rates — and HYSA yields — may instead hold or rise. Neither path is guaranteed; the sequencing guidance below holds under both. The framework's debt-vs-savings sequencing language ("above HYSA yield, below ~7%" threshold for moderate-interest debt) narrows in that environment — what counts as "moderate-interest" today shifts as rates fall, so re-evaluate the debt prioritization stack at each rate-cycle inflection rather than treating the current threshold as static. Not a checking account (no interest, too easy to spend); not invested in equities (wrong time horizon for short-term liquidity).
